title: Working in an Indian Distillery | Craft Beer School
desc: The jobs inside an Indian distillery, from fermentation and stills to maturation and bottling, plus the skills that carry over from brewing.
teaser: A distillery is a brewery with a still on the end. Most of the jobs and most of the skills overlap more than people expect.
standfirst: Indian distilleries employ people across fermentation, distillation, maturation, blending, bottling and quality. Here is what each area involves and how to get into one, especially if you already know some brewing.
sections:
Most spirit made in India starts with molasses, a by-product of sugar production, fermented and distilled to a high-strength neutral spirit. Grain distilleries use cereals such as rice, maize and other grains. A smaller number make malt whisky from malted barley in pot stills. Our guide to molasses versus grain spirit explains the difference.

The type of distillery shapes the jobs. A large molasses plant runs continuous columns around the clock. A malt distillery runs batches through pot stills and puts a lot of effort into casks and maturation.

The first half of making whisky is very close to brewing. Malt or grain is mashed to convert starch to sugar, cooled and fermented with yeast. The result, called wash, is like a strong, unhopped beer. In malt whisky it typically reaches around 7 to 9 per cent alcohol by volume before it goes to the still.

So the skills carry straight across: hygiene, yeast health, temperature control and reading a fermentation. Infection in a fermenter hurts a distillery as much as a brewery, because a still concentrates flavour. It does not remove bad flavour reliably.

• Process operators in mashing, fermentation and distillation, usually on shifts.
  • Stillmen and distillers, who run the stills and make the cuts that separate the heart of the run from the heads and tails.
  • Warehouse and maturation staff, who fill, move, track and sample casks.
  • Blending and sensory teams, who assess spirit and build consistent products.
  • Bottling hall staff, often the largest group in a big plant.
  • Quality control chemists and microbiologists.
  • Engineering and maintenance, which keeps boilers, columns and lines running.

In a large plant these are separate departments with their own managers. In a craft distillery the same handful of people cover most of them. Bottling and quality tend to have the most openings for newcomers, while stillman and blender roles usually go to people who have spent years in the plant.
Excise is part of daily life

Distilleries in India operate under close excise supervision. Spirit movements are recorded and controlled. Excise officials are involved in many routine steps. Anyone working in production learns to keep precise records and to treat a strength reading or a volume as a legal figure, not only a process one. The detailed rules vary by state and change, so the plant's compliance team is the authority on the current procedure.

Indian heat changes maturation. Spirit evaporates from casks much faster than in Scotland, so whisky matures quickly and the warehouse loses more volume each year. Our guide to the angel's share in Indian heat covers why. Warehouse work here means close attention to cask condition, losses and sampling.

Large distilleries run continuously, so production roles usually mean rotating shifts, including nights. Many plants sit outside cities, close to sugar mills or grain supply, which can mean relocating or long commutes. The work involves heat, steam, high-strength spirit and noise from bottling lines.

Safety is taken seriously for good reason. Spirit vapour is flammable, so distilleries control ignition sources strictly, restrict phones and electrical equipment in some zones and train staff on fire procedure. If you join, take that training seriously from the first day.

Craft distilleries are smaller and more varied. One person may mash, run the still and help with bottling in the same week, which is excellent for learning the whole process quickly.

Large distilleries hire chemistry, microbiology, biotechnology, food technology and chemical engineering graduates, plus ITI and diploma holders for operator and maintenance roles. Experience in a brewery or any fermentation plant is a real advantage.

Where many applicants fall short is fermentation itself. They know the still from textbooks but cannot explain why a wash went sour or why yeast stalled. Learning fermentation properly is the most direct way to make yourself useful in the first half of the plant. Our Craft Distilling course (4 weeks, ₹9,999) covers the still side once you have that base.
faqs: Can a brewer work in a distillery?
Yes. Mashing, fermentation, hygiene and yeast handling are shared skills, so brewers often move into distillery production and quality roles.
What degree do I need to work in an Indian distillery?
Chemistry, microbiology, biotechnology, food technology and chemical engineering are common. Operator and maintenance roles often hire ITI and diploma holders.
Why does whisky mature faster in India?
Higher temperatures speed up the interaction between spirit and wood and also raise evaporation losses from the cask.
